idiom_name: const member functions + const data members + value semantics
implementation_notes: The classic structure is largely absorbed by the language: keep the state in private members that only the constructor can initialise, mark every non-mutating member function const so it can be called through const objects and const references, and pass the type by value or by const reference. Since C++11 a const member function on a possibly shared object must be safe to call concurrently without external synchronisation, which is exactly the sharing guarantee this pattern wants. The hand-written form is still needed when a member is mutable (caches, mutexes), when the class must stay polymorphic and open to subclassing, or when copy-on-write internals make const overloading necessary.
pitfalls: const data members delete the copy-assignment operator, which breaks containers and algorithms that assign; const member functions give most of the benefit without that cost.
const is shallow and not transitive: a const member function that returns a non-const pointer (or a non-const reference to a member) hands out write access to a const object.
mutable members used for memoisation must be internally synchronised, otherwise concurrent const calls race while looking read-only (the M&M rule: mutable comes with mutex).

variants.name: constexpr literal type (compile-time values)
variants.idiom_name: constexpr literal type with compile-time construction
variants.implementation_notes: Where the value is known while compiling, the immutable object is a literal type built by a constexpr constructor: the state is fixed before the program runs, may live in read-only memory, and can be used as a template argument or an array bound. This replaces the runtime-constructed object for configuration-like values and removes the copy-assignment question entirely, because the value is never reassigned; the const-qualified runtime form remains the general case for values computed from input.
pitfalls: A constexpr constructor must be evaluable at compile time, so allocation-bearing members (std::string, std::vector) make the type non-literal and rule this variant out.
constexpr on a function does not make runtime objects immutable: called with runtime arguments it is an ordinary function, and only const membership or value semantics fix the state.
